paper_title: How Many Exposures Does a World Model Need? Learning Unseen Game Mechanics at Test Time

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: World models enable agents to plan and learn from imagined experience, but in an unfamiliar environment they must learn its mechanics from limited interaction. A mechanic is a rule for how an action or an interaction changes part of the environment. Each occurrence of a mechanic that the model observes is one exposure. We ask how many exposures a world model needs to predict the effects of a new environment's mechanics. We address this question on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark of interactive games defined by their programs. We introduce MechEval, which labels 69 recurring mechanics across 20 games from these programs. It scores each prediction on the cells the mechanic changes at each exposure. As a test bed, we build WARC (World model for ARC-AGI-3), a 35M-parameter vision transformer that is pretrained on other games and updates all of its parameters after each transition. On held-out games, WARC learns to predict four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy on the cells they change and keeps that accuracy to the end of the recordings. Half of them reach that accuracy within about 80 exposures, in a single play of the game, and without updates only one in seven does at all. In closed-loop play on the public games, WARC-Agent, which pairs WARC with a fixed graph explorer, triples the explorer's official efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, mostly through test-time training. On the hidden games of the Kaggle leaderboard, our entry scores 0.20.

On the hidden games of the Kaggle leaderboard, our entry scores 0.20. 1. Introduction An agent that enters new environment must learn how it works from the little experience it gathers there. How efficiently it learns is central to intelligence, which has been defined as the efficiency of acquiring new skills [15]. ARCAGI-3 measures this efficiency directly, comparing agents and humans by the actions they need to clear each level of interactive games they have never seen [4, 16]. To clear level, an agent must discover the rules of the game, explore it, and find its goal. Exploring and finding the goal both depend on predicting what its actions will do. world model provides these predictions [32, 33], but it is usually learned from 104 to 108 interactions with the environment it models [33]. In new game, as in any new environment, it must instead learn the rules from few interactions and predict their effects in situations it has not seen [62]. Two gaps make this regime hard to study. First, methods differ in what they predict and how they use new evidence, from an inferred context to gradient steps on latent dynamics [62, 92], and have not been compared under common protocol. Second, there is no established way to measure the adaptation itself. Ying et al. [96] call for assessing world models by how efficiently they adapt, but the usual measures do not isolate it. An agents return confounds model learning with exploration and planning [33, 50]. We propose to measure adaptation by how efficiently world model learns the mechanics of the new environment. mechanic is conditional rule for how an action or an interaction changes part of the environment. For example, tile that rotates whatever is placed on it does so wherever it appears. model that has learned the rule can predict its effect in new places, so few transitions inform many predictions [45, 67, 85]. Each occurrence of mechanic adds evidence for one rule, so we count experience in exposures, the occurrences observed so far. Exposure does not depend on the model, so methods can be compared at equal exposure, and accuracy on occurrences in new configurations separates learning the rule from memorizing transitions. We ask: How many exposures to new mechanic does world model need to predict its effects? Each game of ARC-AGI-3 is program, so the rules that act at each step can be read from it. MechEval, an annotator built into the game programs and shown in Fig. 1, applies this measure to ARC-AGI-3. For any transition, it reports which mechanics fire and which cells each one changes. Each prediction is scored on those cells and tracked against the mechanics exposure. With this protocol, we study what makes world model learn fast. Our test bed is WARC (World model for ARCAGI-3), 35M-parameter vision transformer, pretrained on other games, that predicts the next frame in pixel space and updates all of its parameters after each transition. With WARC, we compare two design choices: gradient updates versus recurrent state, and full-parameter updates versus LoRA [38]. Finally, WARC-Agent, WARC inside fixed graph explorer that ranks actions by the novelty of its predicted outcomes, tests whether faster learning carries over to closed-loop play. Our contributions are: MechEval: an annotator built into the game programs that measures per-mechanic prediction accuracy for 69 mechanics in 20 games. WARC: simple vision transformer that learns to predict mechanics reliably in fewer exposures than the baselines. Four in five mechanics reach criterion, half of them within about 80 exposures. WARC-Agent: simplified graph explorer [73] guided by WARC that triples the explorers official score, Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), from 0.15 to 0.46. 2. Related Work Adapting world model to new environment. world model is usually learned from the environment it models. Model-based agents such as DreamerV3 [33] learn world model from 104 to 108 interactions with each game [37, 60, 98]. Pretrained world models transfer across games and tasks but are still finetuned on thousands of transitions or more of each new one [14, 34, 35, 94]. AdaWorld adapts from few interactions by pretraining with latent actions [29]. Test-time adaptation of world models has been studied for changes in known quantity, such as mass, appearance, or layout. In-context methods infer context from recent transitions [52, 62, 68, 74], amortize the update into hypernetwork or mixture of experts [40, 64], or learn from synthetic prior [24]. Gradient-based methods update the model at test time. AdaJEPA does so inside the planning loop [92], others on explored transitions or in residual modules [81, 87], and CAVIA only on context vector [100]. On static ARC puzzles, test-time training on each puzzles demonstrations is the standard recipe [1, 39], and WARC applies it along the stream of game. We compare both forms on the mechanics of unseen games and score the world models predictions rather than an agents return. Learning the rules of game. Game description languages such as VGDL [76] and Autumn [19] write game as set of rules, like our mechanics. Theory-based agents infer such rule set from play as program [85], and languagemodel agents, including several published agents on ARCAGI-3, write and repair it as code [71, 79, 84]. These methods recover the rules explicitly, whereas we ask how many exposures neural world model needs to predict them. Evaluating world models. Evaluation of world models has been extended from visual fidelity to physical understanding [61] and the consistency of game mechanics [55]. ScratchWorld credits prediction only when it computes 2 the fields that an action changes [54], and AutumnBench evaluates prediction and planning after reward-free interaction phase [93]. Ying et al. [96] propose new games under trial budget to assess how efficiently world model adapts. In contrast, MechEval scores each mechanic at each exposure while the model learns, with ground truth from the game programs. Appendix covers other work. 3. Preliminaries Games. Each ARC-AGI-3 game is turn-based environment governed by deterministic program with hidden state st [4]. At every turn, the agent observes frame ot and takes an action at. frame is 6464 grid of cells in 16 colors, and an action is one of up to five keys or click on cell, as in Fig. 1. Each game consists of sequence of levels. level ends once its hidden goal is reached, and the next level applies the same dynamics to new layout. The setting is discrete and deterministic, and since the frame shows the whole board, it is nearly fully observable. Mechanics. As in game description languages [19, 76, 85], mechanic pairs binary condition cm on the state and action with change em to the objects it acts on. It fires whenever cm = 1. Learning games dynamics therefore means learning its mechanics. mechanic is rule as the program implements it, and we measure learning per mechanic. Each mechanic changes only few cells, so most of the frame stays the same. Mechanics also recur during play, at other positions and in later levels. World models and test-time training. world model with parameters θ predicts the next frame from the last frames and actions, ˆot+1 = fθ(oth+1:t, ath+1:t). Such model is usually trained on the environment it models and then kept fixed. Test-time training instead updates θ with selfsupervised loss on the test input before predicting [82]. VARC. VARC [39] applies test-time training to the static puzzles of ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2, and WARC builds on it (Sec. 5). It treats puzzle as an image-to-image task, in which vision transformer predicts the color of each cell of the output grid from the input grid. Each puzzle has its own learned task token that conditions the network. For new puzzle, VARC trains the network and new task token on the two to four demonstration pairs and their rotated, flipped, and recolored copies, then predicts the test output. puzzle is static, with all its demonstrations given at once. The parameters persist along the stream, as in online test-time training [82, 90]. model can instead keep θ fixed and condition on context of recent transitions. In both cases, the model carries what it has learned along the stream. 4. MechEval Our question is how many exposures model needs before it predicts the effect of mechanic in new game. Accuracy over all cells of the frame cannot answer this question for two reasons. First, copying the last frame already predicts 98.8% of the cells correctly, because most cells do not change. Second, an average over game is dominated by its most frequent mechanics. MechEval therefore follows each mechanic separately along the stream of Sec. 3. It scores every occurrence of mechanic, step at which the mechanic fires, on the cells it changes. It reports this accuracy against the models exposures to the mechanic, as in Fig. 1. Annotation. MechEval covers 20 of the 25 public games, with 69 mechanics and 279 human recordings [43], each truncated when level 2 is first completed. Each mechanic produces one type of change, such as the rotation of the key piece when the player steps on tile, or counter that decreases with every move. We first described the mechanics of each game in natural language, from the game code and the screen transitions, in codebook of 107 entries. We checked every entry against the game programs and the recordings, and instrumented the programs to log which mechanics fire at every step and on which objects. Occurrences and exposures are thus read from the program rather than inferred from the frames (Appendix B). For every step of every recording, the ground truth gives the mechanics Mt that fire and, for each, the cells of its objects that change color, with rules for cells that two mechanics share. These are all that MechEval needs from an environment. Other environments can be scored in the same way if their simulator can log them. change that happens only once or twice, such as picking up the only key of level, leaves no later occurrence to predict. We therefore keep mechanic only if it fires at least three times in the median recording that contains it. Exposures to criterion. To summarize each learning curve by one number, we follow trials to criterion from studies of human and animal learning [78]: the number of trials learner needs before its responses meet criterion that the study sets, such as ten correct answers in row. It marks when the predictions of mechanic become reliable rather than how accurate they are on average. We count exposures instead of trials. We define the exposures to criterion (EtC) of mechanic as the first from which its learning curve stays at or above 80% for every later exposure. mechanic whose accuracy is below 80% at its last exposure has not reached the criterion (n.r.), and its EtC is that last exposure. 5. WARC WARC, the base model of our study, builds on VARC. It keeps the vision transformer that predicts the color of each cell, and it learns each new task at test time, as VARC does. The main change is in how it learns. VARC trains on few demonstrations and then answers, whereas WARC predicts each transition of game and then trains on it (Sec. 5.2). WARC also has no task token, so everything it learns about new game is held in its weights. The other changes adapt the model and its data to games (Sec. 5.1). It takes the last frames and actions instead of one grid, patchifies the frames jointly, and is pretrained on human recordings of other games. Tab. 6 lists every difference, including augmentations that rotate the actions with the frames. 5.1. Model WARC is vision transformer [22] that maps the window xt = (oth+1:t, ath+1:t) of the last frames and actions to distribution pθ(ot+1 xt) over the next frame. The distribution factorizes over cells, each with distribution over the 16 colors, and the predicted frame ˆot+1 takes the most probable color at each cell. Both pretraining and test-time training minimize the negative log-likelihood of the observed next frame, which is the sum of the crossentropies of its cells, L(θ) = log pθ(ot+1 xt). (5) The model reads several frames because few state variables are not shown in single frame. The = 3 frames are patchified jointly into 3D patches of 22 cells and three frames, so each token covers the same cells across time. The actions condition every block. No token identifies the game, since new game comes with no identity and the frames show which game it is. 5.2. Learning on the Stream The input of WARC covers only the last frames and actions, so transition outside this window affects prediction only through the updates it has caused. The weights thus play the role of recurrent state, as the weights of the inner model do in test-time training layers [83]. Section 6.4 compares these updates with recurrent state that reads the same transitions. To learn new mechanic from its first few exposures, WARC updates after every transition. To keep the mechanics it has already learned, it also replays earlier transitions. After each transition, it takes 20 gradient steps of Eq. (2) with the loss of Eq. (5), on minibatches of eight drawn from the ten most recent transitions, twenty older ones sampled at random, and their augmented copies. When mechanic fires for the (k+1)-th time, WARC has already trained on all earlier occurrences. All parameters are updated, so new mechanic can change any part of the model. Each transition is augmented with its three rotations, with the click positions rotated with the frames and the four movement keys relabeled, which assumes that these keys move in the four directions. The updates use the pretraining optimizer, Muon with AdamW, at constant learning rate, keeping its state across updates. Appendix gives the architecture and hyperparameters. 6. Experiments on MechEval We address three questions on MechEval. How quickly does WARC learn the mechanics of an unseen game, and how do the alternatives compare (Sec. 6.2)? Does it learn the mechanics or memorize the transitions it has seen (Sec. 6.3)? Which design choices in the model and the update determine its speed (Sec. 6.4)? 6.1. The model starts from its pretrained checkpoint, learns along the recording, and is then discarded. The 25 public games are split into three folds, and each is evaluated with the model pretrained on the human recordings of the other two folds, with augmented copies (Appendix C). Metrics. We report EtC with the fraction of mechanics not reached (n.r., Sec. 4). The false-edit rate (FE) is the fraction of unchanged cells predicted to change, including steps where move is blocked (Appendix F). Kinds of mechanics. To break down the results, we label each mechanic by how it follows from an action (Appendix B). direct mechanic is the effect of key press (15 mechanics) or click (16) on the object it acts on. linked mechanic follows another change of the state, such as marker that moves to the selected piece (10). contact mechanic happens only when the action brings two objects together, such as block that slides when pushed (6). counter is step or budget bar (21), and one autonomous mechanic is an agent that moves on its own. Model selection. The test-time recipe was selected on the five public games not covered by MechEval, so that no evaluated game influenced the choice. Comparisons. All methods receive the same frames and actions and are scored identically. Those that learn by gradient descent also receive WARCs update budget (Sec. 5.2). WARC (scratch) starts from random initialization and measures what the updates learn without pretraining. WARC (GRU) reads the recording through convolutional GRU instead of three frames and is not updated. It tests whether recurrent state can replace the updates. DreamerV3 [33] is latent world model whose recurrent state is recomputed over the last 64 frames, so it adapts in context even without updates. It is pretrained on the same folds, updated under recipe tuned on the same five games as WARCs, and scored on its decoded frames. Statistics. Results are for test-time seed 0 unless stated otherwise. We test this on the direct mechanics, the 15 key and 16 click mechanics, where what is new can be read from the action. We therefore place WARC in fixed explorer, which proposes actions that WARC ranks by the novelty of their predicted outcomes, and call this agent WARC-Agent. We ask whether learning the mechanics in play makes exploration more efficient. 7.1. Setup Agent. The explorer, simplified version of published graph explorer [73], hashes frames into states, records the actions tried in each state, and returns along known paths to states with untried actions. Its actions are the available keys, click on each connected component of the frame, and grid of 64 clicks, tried in priority groups. Without model, the explorer picks an untried action of the current group at random. With WARC, it ranks the untried actions of the current group, as in model-based exploration [77]. WARC predicts the next frame for each of these actions and extends the most novel ones by second step. The explorer takes the action whose predicted frame differs most from the frames seen in the level. Protocol. Each agent plays each of the 25 public games with seeds 0 to 9, and every measure is read from its first 1,000 actions. Unlike in Sec. 6, WARC learns from the agents own transitions. 7.2. Limitations MechEval covers levels 1 and 2 of the 20 public games whose changes can be attributed to single objects. It scores mechanic only in the situations that the human recordings reach, so reaching the criterion is weaker than learning the rule in general. This work does not model the goal of game, which changes once per level and so falls outside the recurring mechanics we evaluate. In closed-loop play, the action selector is hand-designed and shared across conditions, so our claims concern the world model rather than the agent. Even with an oracle world model, the explorer clears no level in five games. All results come from one benchmark of deterministic, discrete games on 6464 grid. Whether updating the weights after each transition works as well with continuous or stochastic dynamics is untested. 8 9. Conclusion We asked how many exposures world model needs to predict the mechanics of new game. Within single play of an unseen game, WARC brings four in five mechanics to criterion, half of them within about 80 exposures, and without updates only one in seven reaches it. One play has far fewer interactions than the 104 to 108 from which world models usually learn their environment. What WARC learns comes from each mechanics own transitions and carries over to other recordings of the game, including moves it has not seen. The speed comes from pretraining on other games and from gradient update after each transition. The recurrent state of WARC (GRU), which reads the same transitions, does not replace these updates at this pretraining scale. With the action selector fixed, WARC-Agent triples the efficiency score of the explorer alone, mostly through test-time training, and an oracle world model triples it again. Higher scores need both world model that learns faster and an action selector that aims at the goal of each game. Unlike the score of level, MechEval shows which mechanics model learns and after how many exposures. It can score any model that predicts the next frame, including the programs that language-model agents write to simulate game [17, 53, 71]. These agents could in turn use world model learned in play as simulator, to test the actions they propose or to roll out plans toward goal. Other environments, such as robotics simulators, can be scored in the same way if they log which mechanics fire and what each one changes, which we leave to future work.

sections.title: Appendix
sections.content: A. Kaggle Submission Submission. Our entry to the ARC-AGI-3 competition on Kaggle runs WARC-Agent (Appendix I), in which WARC ranks the explorers actions and updates with the recipe of Sec. 5.2 after every valid transition. The competition scores agents on 110 hidden games, none of which is among the 25 public games. Since pretraining on more games helps (Appendix H), the submitted model is pretrained on all 25 public games with the recipe of Appendix C. The rest of the paper holds out games by fold, so that every evaluated game is unseen in pretraining, as the hidden games are. The notebook, the agent, the pretraining and test-time training code, and the weights are at https://github.com/third-intelligence/WARC. We will release the annotations and the scorer of MechEval. The submission scores 0.20 on the public leaderboard, which uses half of the hidden games. The hidden games are not public, so we cannot tell how they differ from the public games, and the score on them may differ widely from our results on the public games. Time budget. The notebook plays the hidden games one at time on one RTX PRO 6000 Server Edition GPU without network access and must finish within nine hours. We gave the games 8.6 hours in total, so each game gets about 280 s. We timed the notebook on the same GPU type in two games played with keys. In these games, an action takes 0.74 s, most of it for the 20 gradient steps after each transition, so game gets about 380 actions. Agent Explorer. The explorer is simplified version of published graph explorer [73]. It keeps graph of the states reached in the current level and the actions tried in each. state is keyed by hash of the frame, with the status bars masked as in the first frame of the level, and by the set of available actions. The actions are the available keys, one click at the center of each connected component of the frame, and fixed grid of 64 clicks. They are tried in priority order, first the keys and the components of at most 1,024 cells, then the grid, then the larger components. In state with untried actions, the explorer chooses among the untried actions of the highest open priority group, uniformly when it has no world model. Otherwise it moves along known edges to the nearest untried action, by priority and then by distance. If none is reachable, it retries the least-tried actions of the current state. The published explorer adds hand-set rules on the frame. It detects status bars by their shape and position, sorts the clicks into five groups by color and size, with segments of non-gray colors and medium size 28 first, and opens the groups one at time. Our explorer instead orders the clicks by size and masks only thin bars along the top and bottom edges. It clicks at the center of each component and on fixed grid rather than at random cell of each segment, adds the available actions to the state key, and never rebuilds its graph within level. Additional Related Work Video world models. Trained on large video and interaction datasets, video world models simulate real-world interaction [95], physical scenes [63], and navigation [8]. In games, GameGAN [47], Genie [11], GameNGen [86], DIAMOND [2], Muse [44], and Matrix-Game [36] simulate the games they were trained on. Latent world models such as DINO-WM [99] and V-JEPA 2 [6] predict in the feature space of pretrained encoder and plan with them. These models are finetuned for new domain or applied to it without updates. We instead study how world model adapts online to an unseen game. Test-time training and continual learning. Test-time training updates model on each test input with self-supervised loss [82], and dynamic evaluation adapts sequence model to the sequence it is predicting [49]. TENT updates only the normalization parameters on unlabeled test data [88]. Test-time training layers make the hidden state of sequence model the weights of an inner model, updated by gradient step on each token [83]. LaCT updates them on large chunks [97]. Such layers also generate minute-long videos [18]. On video stream, model can also be trained online on each frame [91]. Over stream of updates, continual learning limits forgetting by replaying earlier data [72] or by protecting important weights [48]. Continual test-time adaptation restores part of the source weights [90]. Plasticity can also be lost as training continues [21]. WARC replays earlier transitions in every update (Sec. 5.2). Exploration. Curiosity-driven agents reward transitions that their own model predicts poorly [12, 65], and Plan2Explore plans toward states where an ensemble of world models disagrees [77]. Go-Explore keeps an archive of visited states and returns to promising ones before exploring from them [23]. Our agent combines graph of visited states with ranking of untried actions by the novelty of their predicted outcomes (Appendix I). ARC puzzles. Vision transformers such as VARC [39], RoSeViT [57], and TraceViT [56] cast puzzle as image-to-image translation. Loop-OWM instead learns composable, object-centric world model of puzzles rule [28]. Agents on ARC-AGI-3. Besides the agents cited in Sec. 2, published agents have frontier language model write and repair programmatic world model [70], as in OPINE-World [17] and Tycho [53]. Others run language model within harness with memory, feedback, or curriculum [5, 13, 25, 26, 46, 75]. Agents without language model explore with graph over states [73] or train predictor from scratch on each game, like StochasticGoose [42, 80]. We compare with both in closed-loop play (Sec. 7). Rule changes and rule discovery. Boult et al. [10] formalize novelty, and NovGrid [7], NovelGridworlds [30], NovelGym [31], and NovPhy [27] inject controlled rule changes into grid worlds and physics puzzles. DiG-bench makes rule discovery the task itself [9]. MechEval instead follows each mechanic of an existing game across its occurrences.
